opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, Peter. It's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that we're in the middle of an experiment nobody signed up for.

Throughout history, every time we invented a tool that takes over a mental function, the brain adapted. Writing is the classic example. Socrates complained that writing would ruin memory, and in a sense he was right. We don't memorize epic poems anymore. But we gained something: we could store far more knowledge than any single brain could hold, and we freed up capacity for other things.

What's different now is the scope and the speed. GPS took over navigation, and we have studies showing that people who rely on it heavily engage the parts of the brain involved in spatial memory, like the hippocampus, less. Search engines took over recall. Now we have tools that don't just remember for us or guide us. They reason, write, and make suggestions about what we should do. We're outsourcing judgment, not just storage.

From a neuroscience perspective, the brain is very economical. If it doesn't need to do something, it stops investing in it. So the question isn't whether we'll lose some abilities. We will. The question is which ones we're willing to lose and what we do with the freed-up space.

My concern is that decision-making is close to the core of what makes us feel like ourselves. When you make a choice, even a bad one, you own it. You learn from it, and it shapes your identity. If an algorithm picks your restaurant, your route, your partner, your words, you can end up with a life that's very efficient but that you don't feel you authored. People report more satisfaction with choices they made themselves, even when an outside option is objectively better.

There's an upside I find exciting, though. If we're deliberate about it, these tools can act like an external prefrontal cortex. They can help us keep long-term goals in mind when our impulses pull us elsewhere, and they can compensate for biases we know we have. The tool is neutral. What matters is whether we use it to augment ourselves or to replace ourselves.

So my practical advice is to keep some things deliberately "manual." Pick the domains that matter most to your sense of who you are, and keep doing them yourself, even if it's slower. Let the machines handle the rest. That way you get the benefits without quietly handing over the parts of the human experience that make it worth having.

r001.rationale: The response says the brain stops investing in functions it no longer needs and explicitly predicts that people will lose some abilities as technology takes over thinking.

r002.rationale: It discusses GPS reducing engagement in spatial memory, but does not identify lost serendipitous discoveries caused by avoiding navigation mistakes.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Peter. So I think about this as a neuroscientist, and the first thing I'd say is that outsourcing thinking is not new. We've been doing it forever. Writing was outsourcing memory. Socrates was famously worried that writing would make people forget things, and he was right, we did get worse at memorizing. But we got something else in return. The calculator outsourced arithmetic. GPS outsourced navigation, and there are studies showing that people who rely on GPS have a hippocampus that's less engaged when they move through a city. So the brain really does respond. Whatever you stop using, it stops investing in.

What's different now is the kind of thing we're outsourcing. Memory, arithmetic, navigation, those are tools. They sit around the thinking. What we're handing over now is closer to the thinking itself: forming an opinion, weighing options, deciding what matters. And that touches something the brain uses to build identity. A lot of who you think you are comes from the little decisions you make all day, and from the effort of making them. When you ask a machine which restaurant, which route, which argument is right, you're not just saving time. You're skipping the part where your brain learns what you prefer.

Now, I'm not a pessimist about it. In the lab we see that the brain is incredibly good at adapting to a new tool and then finding new things to do with the freed-up capacity. The risk is not that we become stupid. The risk is that we become homogeneous. If everyone asks the same system the same question and gets roughly the same answer, you lose the variance, and variance is where creativity and disagreement and progress come from. Human thinking is noisy, it's biased, it's slow, but that noise is a feature. It's how one person in a room ends up seeing something the other nine missed.

So my honest answer is that the human experience is getting more comfortable and less effortful, and effort was doing more for us than we realized. The people who come out ahead will be the ones who deliberately keep some friction in their lives. They use the tools, but they still do the hard version sometimes, the way you might walk even though you own a car. Not because it's efficient, but because the walking is the point.

r001.rationale: The response says writing made people worse at memorizing and that the brain invests less in abilities it stops using, with GPS as an example of reduced hippocampal engagement.

r002.rationale: It discusses GPS reducing hippocampal engagement, but does not identify lost serendipitous discoveries caused by avoiding navigation mistakes.

astra-6.text:
I think it changes what we consider worth doing with our brains. We’ve always outsourced things. Writing lets us put memories outside our heads. A calculator lets us avoid doing arithmetic. And usually, when we stop doing one kind of work, we gain the ability to do something else.

But there’s a difference between outsourcing a calculation and outsourcing the decision about what matters to you. If a system gives you directions, you can judge whether you arrived where you wanted to go. If it tells you what career to pursue, who to date, or what to believe, checking the answer is much harder. You may start adopting its criteria without realizing it.

So the question is: which parts of thinking do we want to preserve, even when a machine can do them more efficiently? Sometimes the effort is part of the value. Working through a disagreement can change you. Struggling to articulate an idea can help you discover what you actually think. Getting the finished answer doesn’t necessarily give you that experience.

I’m excited about having tools that expand what we can understand. But I’d want us to remain active participants—to be able to question the answer, and especially to decide which questions deserve our attention.

r001.rationale: The response warns that people may adopt a system’s criteria and miss the value of thinking through ideas, but it does not say outsourcing thinking diminishes human cognitive function.

r002.rationale: It mentions directions, but does not identify lost serendipitous discovery from technology preventing navigation mistakes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it changes what we need to be good at. When you outsource memory to your phone, you don’t suddenly stop thinking. But you change the things you practice. You get very good at finding information, and perhaps less good at remembering it. And the same thing can happen with judgment: if something is always giving you an answer, you have fewer opportunities to work through the uncertainty yourself.

There’s a tremendous benefit to that. You don’t want every person to have to discover everything from scratch. Language, books, education—these are all ways of using thinking that happened outside your own head. So outsourcing thought isn’t entirely new. What’s different is that now the tool can participate in the decision. It can suggest what you should say, what you should buy, even what you should want.

And that’s where I think the interesting question is. Are you using it to accomplish a goal you chose, or is it gradually choosing the goal for you? Those can feel very similar in the moment. A recommendation is convenient. A thousand recommendations can start to shape a life.

So I’m excited about having tools that help us think. But I would want us to preserve the ability to pause and ask, ‘Why am I doing this? Is this actually what I want?’ Because getting an answer more easily is valuable only if you still have some ownership of the question.

r001.rationale: The response says outsourcing memory can make people less good at remembering, and relying on answers can reduce practice in working through uncertainty themselves.

r002.rationale: It does not identify fewer navigation mistakes or reduced serendipitous discovery as a loss caused by technology.
